front_blocks.md: Define **function**.

back_blocks.md: A **function** is a mapping in which every 'input' maps to exactly one 'output'.
Functions are written as `\text{f}\left(x\right)`, or in the alternative form `\text{f} : x \mapsto x^{2} - 3 x + 2`.

cards.front_md: Define **function**.
cards.back_md:
A **function** is a mapping in which every 'input' maps to exactly one 'output'.

Functions are written as `\text{f}\left(x\right)`, or in the alternative form `\text{f} : x \mapsto x^{2} - 3 x + 2`.

front_blocks.md: Which types of mapping are functions?

back_blocks.md: **One-to-one** and **many-to-one** mappings.
One-to-many and many-to-many are not, because a single input would have more than one output.

cards.front_md: Which types of mapping are functions?
cards.back_md:
**One-to-one** and **many-to-one** mappings.

One-to-many and many-to-many are not, because a single input would have more than one output.

front_blocks.md: The `\_\_\_\_\_\_` of a function is the set of allowed inputs, and the `\_\_\_\_\_\_` is the set of all possible outputs.

back_blocks.md: The **domain** of a function is the set of allowed inputs, and the **range** is the set of all possible outputs.
The range depends on the domain: change which inputs are allowed and the outputs change with them.

front_blocks.md: Why is squaring a **many-to-one** mapping?

back_blocks.md: Because different inputs can give the same output: both $2$ and $- 2$ map to $4$.
It is still a function, since each individual input has only one output.

cards.front_md: Why is squaring a **many-to-one** mapping?
cards.back_md:
Because different inputs can give the same output: both $2$ and $- 2$ map to $4$.

It is still a function, since each individual input has only one output.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
`\text{f}\left(x\right) = x^{2}` on its own is a fully defined function.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A function is not fully defined until its **domain** has been stated.
Without it you cannot say what the range is, or whether the function is one-to-one.

front_blocks.md: How can restricting the domain change a function?

back_blocks.md: It can turn a **many-to-one** function into a **one-to-one** one.
`\text{f}\left(x\right) = x^{2}` is many-to-one over all real $x$, but restricting it to $x \geq 0$ makes it one-to-one.

front_blocks.md: How do you work out the range of a function?

back_blocks.md: Find the outputs that the stated domain actually produces, sketching the graph where that helps.
For `\text{f}\left(x\right) = x^{2}` with $x \in ℝ$ the range is `\text{f}\left(x\right) \geq 0`, because a square is never negative.

front_blocks.md: Define **composite function**.

back_blocks.md: A **composite function** is one function applied after another, with the output of the first becoming the input of the second.

It can be written `\text{fg}\left(x\right)`, `\text{f}\left(\text{g}\left(x\right)\right)` or `\left(\text{f} \circ \text{g}\right)\left(x\right)`, all meaning "$\text{f}$ of `\text{g}\left(x\right)`".

front_blocks.md: In `\text{fg}\left(x\right)`, which function is applied first?

back_blocks.md: $\text{g}$, the one closest to the variable.
You work outwards: apply $\text{g}$ to $x$ first, then apply $\text{f}$ to whatever that produces.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
`\text{fg}\left(x\right)` and `\text{gf}\left(x\right)` always give the same result.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The order in which the functions are applied changes the answer, so the two are usually different.
They can happen to agree for particular pairs of functions, but that cannot be assumed.

front_blocks.md: Applying a function to its own output, `\text{ff} \left(x\right)`, is written as `\_\_\_\_\_\_`.

back_blocks.md: Applying a function to its own output, `\text{ff}\left(x\right)`, is written as `\text{f}^{2}\left(x\right)`.
This means apply $\text{f}$ twice, not square the answer.

front_blocks.md: Why might `\text{fg} \left(x\right)` exist when `\text{gf} \left(x\right)` does not?

back_blocks.md: Because the output of the first function has to be an allowed input for the second.
The range of $\text{g}$ must lie inside the domain of $\text{f}$, and that can hold one way round without holding the other.

front_blocks.md: Given `\text{f} \left(x\right) = 2 x` and `\text{g} \left(x\right) = x + 3`, what is `\text{fg} \left(x\right)`?

back_blocks.md: `\text{fg}\left(x\right) = 2\left(x + 3\right) = 2 x + 6`.
Taking them the other way round gives `\text{gf}\left(x\right) = 2 x + 3`, which is a different function.

front_blocks.md: Define **inverse function**.

back_blocks.md: The **inverse function** `\text{f}^{- 1}\left(x\right)` undoes what $\text{f}$ does, taking each output back to the input it came from.
It exists only if $\text{f}$ is **one-to-one**.

cards.front_md: Define **inverse function**.
cards.back_md:
The **inverse function** `\text{f}^{- 1}\left(x\right)` undoes what $\text{f}$ does, taking each output back to the input it came from.

It exists only if $\text{f}$ is **one-to-one**.

front_blocks.md: Why must a function be one-to-one to have an inverse?

back_blocks.md: Because the inverse has to send each output back to a **single** input.
If two inputs shared an output, the inverse would not know which of them to return to, and so would not itself be a function.

cards.front_md: Why must a function be one-to-one to have an inverse?
cards.back_md:
Because the inverse has to send each output back to a **single** input.

If two inputs shared an output, the inverse would not know which of them to return to, and so would not itself be a function.

front_blocks.md: A function followed by its inverse returns the original input:
`\text{ff}^{- 1} \left(x\right) = \text{f}^{- 1} \text{f} \left(x\right) = \_\_\_\_\_\_`

back_blocks.md: `\text{ff}^{- 1}\left(x\right) = \text{f}^{- 1}\text{f}\left(x\right) = x`
This is exactly what "undoing" means, and it holds for every value of $x$ in the domain.

front_blocks.md: How is the graph of `\text{f}^{- 1}\left(x\right)` related to the graph of `\text{f}\left(x\right)`?

back_blocks.md: It is the reflection in the line $y = x$.
Reflecting in that line swaps the two coordinates of every point, which is precisely what taking the inverse does.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The domain of $\text{f}^{-1}$ is the range of $\text{f}$.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The two swap over, because the outputs of $\text{f}$ are exactly the inputs of $\text{f}^{-1}$.
The domain of $\text{f}$ is likewise the range of $\text{f}^{-1}$.

front_blocks.md: How do you find an inverse function algebraically?

back_blocks.md: Write `y = \text{f}\left(x\right)`, then rearrange to make $x$ the subject.
Rewrite the result in function notation, remembering to give its domain as well.

front_blocks.md: How can an inverse function be used to solve `\text{f} \left(x\right) = 5`?

back_blocks.md: The solution is `x = \text{f}^{- 1}\left(5\right)`.
Applying $\text{f}^{-1}$ to both sides undoes $\text{f}$ on the left, leaving $x$ on its own.

front_blocks.md: Define the **modulus** of a number.

back_blocks.md: The **modulus** makes any input **positive**: `\left| x \right| = x` when $x \geq 0$, and `\left| x \right| = - x` when $x < 0$.
So `\left| 5 \right|` and `\left| - 5 \right|` are both $5$, and it is also called the **absolute value**.

front_blocks.md: How do you sketch `y = \left| \text{f} \left(x\right) \right|` from the graph of `y = \text{f} \left(x\right)`?

back_blocks.md: Draw `y = \text{f} \left(x\right)` first, then **reflect** every part lying below the $x$-axis up in the $x$-axis.
Anything already on or above the axis is left exactly as it is.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The graph of `y = \text{f} \left( \left| x \right| \right)` can never go below the $x$-axis.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
That is true of `y = \left| \text{f} \left(x\right) \right|`, whose outputs are all made positive.
`y = \text{f} \left( \left| x \right| \right)` changes only which value goes in, so its outputs can still be negative; what it is guaranteed instead is **symmetry** about the $y$-axis.

front_blocks.md: Complete the vertex of the graph of `y = a \left| x + p \right| + q`:

back_blocks.md: The completed vertex is:
`\text{vertex} = \left( - p , q \right)`
The sign flips inside the modulus, exactly as it does in the completed square form `a \left( x + p \right)^{2} + q`.

front_blocks.md: How many roots can the graph of `y = a \left| x + p \right| + q` have?

back_blocks.md: **Nought, one or two**, depending on where the vertex sits and which way the graph opens.
A V-shaped graph with its vertex above the $x$-axis has none, a vertex on the axis gives exactly one, and a vertex below it gives two.

front_blocks.md: Two non-parallel straight lines meet once. Why can an equation involving a modulus have more solutions than that?

back_blocks.md: Because the modulus **reflects part of a graph** upwards, and the reflected piece can cross the other graph as well.
That produces an intersection the unreflected lines never had.

front_blocks.md: What should you do before solving a modulus equation algebraically?

back_blocks.md: **Sketch both graphs**, including the reflected parts, and locate the intersections.
The sketch tells you how many solutions there should be, and therefore which algebraic answers to keep.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Every solution of $x - 4 = 2 x - 5$ is also a solution of `\left|x - 4\right| = 2 x - 5`.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
$x = 1$ satisfies the first, but `\left|1 - 4\right| = 3` while `2 \left(1\right) - 5 = - 3`, so it fails the second.

front_blocks.md: How do you solve `\left|\text{f} \left(x\right)\right| = \text{g} \left(x\right)`, with a modulus on one side only?

back_blocks.md: Solve both `\text{f}\left(x\right) = \text{g}\left(x\right)` and `- \text{f}\left(x\right) = \text{g}\left(x\right)`.
Then test each answer in the original equation, because a modulus can never be negative, so any root making `\text{g}\left(x\right)` negative has to be thrown out.
